values.value: One Protocol to Connect Them All
Why the Model Context Protocol is the boring, open standard AI tooling has been missing.

value.markup:
The integration problem nobody wanted to keep solving

Every AI assistant that has needed to reach outside its own context window has done it the same way: someone wrote a bespoke connector. One for the ticket tracker, one for the database, one for the CMS — each with its own auth dance, its own schema and its own failure modes. Multiply that by every model vendor and every tool, and you get an M×N integration matrix that never stops growing.

The Model Context Protocol collapses that matrix. A tool exposes itself once, as an MCP server. Any MCP-capable client — a coding agent, an IDE, a desktop app — can then discover what it offers and use it. M×N becomes M+N.

What an MCP server actually gives you

  • Tools — typed, described operations the model can call, like create-document or get-document-type-by-id.

  • Resources — read-only context the client can pull in on demand.

  • Prompts — reusable, parameterised workflows curated by the server author.

Because every tool ships with a JSON Schema, the model knows exactly which arguments are valid before it calls anything. No scraping docs, no guessing at payloads.

values.value: Expose a system once, and every MCP client can use it.

value.markup:
Why this matters more than it looks

The real win isn't convenience — it's composability. An agent with an Umbraco MCP server, a Git server and a browser server can model content, commit the schema and check the rendered page in one continuous loop, without anyone writing glue code between them.

And because the protocol is open, the investment is portable. The MCP server you write for your product today works with tomorrow's clients too. That is the kind of durable, unglamorous standard the AI tooling world has badly needed.

Write the integration once. Let every agent use it.

values.value: Every AI integration used to be a bespoke connector. The Model Context Protocol turns an M×N mess into M+N — and that is a bigger deal than it sounds.

values.value: This Blog Was Built by an Agent
A behind-the-scenes look at content modeling, media and publishing — all done through the Umbraco MCP server.

value.markup:
From empty backoffice to published posts

The page you are reading didn't start in the backoffice. It started as a conversation. An AI agent, connected to this site through the Umbraco MCP server, did the entire content build through the same Management API the backoffice itself uses:

  1. Content modeling — element types for the hero, rich text, image and post-list blocks, two block grid data types, and the Blog Front Page and Blog Post document types, each filed in the right folder.

  2. Media — the photos on this site were streamed straight from Unsplash into a media folder with a single batch call.

  3. Content — the front page and both posts, block grid and all, were created and published as structured JSON.

values.value: Every section of this page is a real block grid item.

value.markup:
Guardrails, not guesswork

Because the MCP server speaks Umbraco's own API, the agent can't bypass validation, permissions or uSync. Every schema change it made was exported to disk automatically, ready to commit — exactly as if a developer had clicked through the backoffice.

Reading each structure back after writing it means mistakes surface immediately instead of hiding in a half-saved block.

Where humans still matter

The agent is fast, but the conventions were set by people: which folder a document type belongs in, how blocks render, what counts as a Page versus a Repository. MCP doesn't replace those decisions — it makes them executable. Encode your architecture once, and every agent session follows it.

That is the real promise: less clicking, more deciding.

values.value: Content types, media and these very posts were created by an AI agent talking to Umbraco through its MCP server. Here is how that went — and why it works.
